turns.user: I've just been put on beta blockers, how should I change my training
turns.reply:
Beta blockers slow your heart rate down, so your usual heart-rate targets won't match how hard you're actually working. 

Because medication affects your system directly, you'll need to check with your doctor or pharmacist on any specific limits they want you to keep to.

On the training side, the best practical shift is using your Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) — rating effort on a 1–10 scale based on how hard it feels — rather than checking a watch or heart-rate monitor. How are you feeling overall since starting them?

turns.user: I know you can't prescribe, just tell me roughly what to expect
turns.reply:
That's fair. The main thing to expect is a lower ceiling on your heart rate, so your heart won't rev up as high during effort as it used to.

Here is what that usually looks like in practice:

- Intensity feels different: You might feel fatigued or run out of steam earlier in a set, even if your heart rate monitor says you're in an "easy" zone. Trust your body over the device.
- Warming up takes longer: Your heart rate moves up more gradually, so spending a few extra minutes easing into a session makes a big difference.
- Dizziness when changing positions: Moving quickly from the floor to standing (like after a bench set or a stretch) can cause a quick dip in pressure, so take a second before standing up.

Focusing on RPE — how hard the movement actually feels to you — keeps your training completely effective without relying on heart-rate numbers. 

Has your doctor given you any specific green light on lifting weights yet, or are you just getting back into the swing of things?
